name: Subdermal Current Lance SCL-1 'Needlepoint'
description:
The SCL-1 is a slender penetrating weapon — functionally a reinforced spike 22cm in length — constructed from a non-conductive ceramic composite sheath over a tungsten-alloy core that serves as an electrode. Upon penetration of the target's skin, the weapon delivers a precisely directed electrical current along the insertion channel, propagating through tissue fluid and targeting conductive pathways — nerves, blood vessels, and implant wiring — rather than simply burning the entry point. The result is a deeply internal electrical injury that causes systemic nerve disruption, implant damage, and in sustained contact, cardiac and neurological cascade effects that are diagnostically consistent with medical emergencies rather than assault.

The SCL-1 was developed within LAZARUS PHARMACEUTICALS' research division as a tool for studying in-vivo electrical propagation through augmented tissue — a legitimate research application that was quietly repurposed. The weapon is powered by a slim handle unit that houses a compressed capacitor bank, delivering between one and five joules of current per activation with a charge cycle of approximately 0.4 seconds. The handle is designed to resemble a medical injector at casual inspection, and the ceramic sheath provides no metallic signature under standard scanner profiles.

The weapon's most controversial feature is its documented effectiveness against augmented individuals specifically. Neural implants, subdermal communication arrays, and myoelectric muscle enhancers all provide additional conductive pathways that amplify internal current propagation, meaning the SCL-1 causes significantly greater damage to augmented targets than to unaugmented ones. This inversion of the typical augmentation-as-protection dynamic has made the weapon both feared and sought after in contexts where augmented operatives represent the primary threat.
specifications: spike length: 22cm spike material: Tungsten-alloy electrode core, ceramic composite sheath handle length: 14cm power source: Compressed capacitor bank output range: 1–5 joules per activation charge cycle: 0.4 seconds scanner profile: Minimal metallic signature (ceramic sheath) weight: 290g disguise profile: Medical injector form factor
tactical_use: Operators use the SCL-1 in close-contact assassination and targeted incapacitation of augmented security personnel. The spike is inserted in joint gaps, the neck, or the inner arm where skin is thin and vascular density is high. Against augmented targets, even a partial penetration into subcutaneous tissue is sufficient for implant disruption at higher current settings. The medical-device appearance allows concealed carry through many security checkpoints. Operators typically strike once and withdraw, relying on the systemic cascade effects to develop over 30–90 seconds rather than requiring sustained contact.
cultural_context: The SCL-1 is discussed in GLMZ's augmentation communities with particular alarm — for heavily augmented individuals, it represents a specific existential threat that standard protective measures do not address. Anti-augmentation extremist groups have been documented acquiring SCL-1 units as ideological weapons, framing their use as 'purification' actions. Among professional operators, it is associated with a very specific kind of cold professionalism — the willingness to kill through what looks like a medical instrument. LAZARUS PHARMACEUTICALS has never publicly acknowledged the weapon's existence.
known_users: Black market weapons dealers (as high-value trade items)
story_hooks: A prominent augmentation rights advocate is found dead of what the coroner rules a cardiac event — but a contact in the medical examiner's office noticed unusual internal burn patterns consistent with subdermal electrical injury and quietly passed the information along.

A shipment of SCL-1 units was intercepted by municipal authorities and logged into evidence — but the evidence locker was accessed three days later, and the weapons are gone. Someone inside law enforcement is distributing them, and the intended recipients are not yet known.

A player character with significant augmentation begins experiencing intermittent implant failures — subtle at first, then cascading. A street medic examining them finds a healed penetration wound they don't remember receiving. Someone used an SCL-1 on them weeks ago, and the damage is only now propagating through their systems.
related_entities: CortexDynamics Apex Drive Performance Neural BCI

physical_description.visual_profile: A deceptively clinical instrument resembling a medical auto-injector or pharmaceutical delivery pen. The spike is nearly invisible in its thinness—a barely-there needle profile that betrays nothing of its lethal internal architecture. The overall silhouette is elongated and slender, designed to vanish in a closed fist or medical kit.
physical_description.dimensions: Total length: 36cm (22cm spike + 14cm handle). Spike diameter: 3–4mm. Handle width: 2.5cm. Compact enough to palm or conceal in a medical pouch.
physical_description.weight_description: Deceptively light in hand—290g feels almost insubstantial, like holding a fountain pen filled with mercury. The weight distribution is balanced slightly toward the handle, giving it a clinician's precision grip rather than a weapon's authority.
physical_description.primary_material: Tungsten-alloy electrode core sheathed in non-conductive ceramic composite. The handle is polymer-based with integrated capacitor bank—industrial-grade thermoplastic reinforced with carbon strands.
physical_description.finish: Matte ceramic on the spike with a barely-perceptible gradient from opaque ivory to translucent at the needle point. The handle is satin-finish medical white with faint hairline scratches from field use. The capacitor housing shows subtle thermal discoloration from repeated charging cycles.
physical_description.color_scheme: Clinical white and cool gray—the aesthetic of pharmaceutical precision. The spike tip fades to near-translucence. Faint traces of oxidized copper visible at the handle/spike junction where the electrode wiring meets the sheath.
physical_description.grip_texture: Smooth medical-grade polymer with a subtle knurled section in the mid-handle for tactile indexing without visual disruption. The surface has a slightly tacky finish to prevent slip—mimics surgical instrument design.
distinctive_features: Needle-thin spike that appears almost fragile at casual inspection
Minimal electrode contacts recessed into the handle—barely visible grooves
Faint LED indicator (recessed flush with the polymer) glows soft red when capacitor bank is charged; invisible from certain angles
Deliberate medicinal branding: subtle LAZARUS PHARMA glyph etched near the base in microscopic text
Thermal stress lines radiating from the capacitor chamber—evidence of rapid charging cycles
Slight ceramic texture variation along the spike shaft from manufacturing, resembling natural material variation
No guard, no crosspiece—pure hypodermic form factor
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: LAZARUS PHARMACEUTICALS logo (stylized helix) etched in 2mm text on the handle's lower third, positioned to be read when held in clinical delivery position. Serial number stamped in microdots on the capacitor housing—visible only under magnification. No barcode or QR code; completely analog and non-scannable.
physical_description.condition_typical: Field-worn but meticulously maintained. The ceramic shows microscopic stress fractures from impact during extraction post-strike, but the handle is kept clean—operators understand that residue can leave evidence. Microscopic blood traces may be present on the spike despite cleaning; ceramic is porous enough to retain biological material in deep micro-fractures.

image_prompt: Product photography of the Subdermal Current Lance SCL-1, displayed horizontally on a dark gunmetal surface. The weapon lies at a slight angle, its nearly-invisible ceramic spike catching dramatic side-lighting that reveals its translucent needle profile—barely-there surgical precision. The polymer handle glows faintly under cool LED work-lighting, revealing subtle thermal stress marks and the recessed charge indicator. A chrome-gloved finger (augmented with visible subcutaneous circuitry lines visible through translucent palm skin) hovers near the handle for scale. Shallow depth of field keeps the spike needle-sharp in focus while background blurs. The aesthetic is clinical dystopia—pharmaceutical precision meets lethal intent. Cinematic side-rim lighting throws the spike's thinness into stark relief, emphasizing its hypodermic lethality. Medical-device color palette: clinical whites, cool grays, faint copper oxidation visible at electrode junction. No context clues—pure weapon isolation. GLMZ aesthetic: functionality over form, designed to pass as medical equipment. --ar 3:2 --v 6
